properties.headline: Special Marine Warning issued September 11 at 9:29AM CDT until September 11 at 11:00AM CDT by NWS Mobile AL
properties.description:
SMWMOB

The National Weather Service in Mobile has issued a

* Special Marine Warning for...
Coastal waters from Okaloosa-Walton County Line to Pensacola FL out
20 NM...
Coastal waters from Pensacola FL to Pascagoula MS out 20 NM...
Pensacola Bay Area including Santa Rosa Sound...
Waters from Okaloosa-Walton County Line to Pensacola FL from 20 to
60 NM...
Waters from Pensacola FL to Pascagoula MS from 20 to 60 NM...

* Until 1100 AM CDT.

* At 929 AM CDT, strong thunderstorms capable of producing
waterspouts were located along a line extending from Pensacola Bay
to 17 nm southeast of Perdido Pass to 29 nm south of Farewell Buoy,
moving east at 30 knots.

HAZARD...Waterspouts and wind gusts 34 knots or greater.

SOURCE...Radar.

IMPACT...Waterspouts can easily overturn boats and create locally
hazardous seas. Small craft could be damaged in briefly
higher winds and suddenly higher waves.

Pensacola Bay, Navarre Beach, Big Lagoon, West Santa Rosa Sound,
Pensacola Beach, Oriskany Reef, Pensacola Pass, Fort Walton Liberty
Ship Reef, and Fort Pickens.

overturn boats and create locally hazardous seas. Seek safe harbor
immediately.

Frequent lightning is occurring with these storms. If caught on the
open water stay below deck if possible, keep away from ungrounded
metal objects.

properties.headline: Extreme Heat Warning issued September 11 at 10:13AM AST until September 11 at 5:00PM AST by NWS San Juan PR
properties.description:
* WHAT...This level of heat can affect anyone without effective
cooling and/or adequate hydration.

* WHERE...A portion of Puerto Rico.

* WHEN...Until 5 PM AST this afternoon.

* IMPACTS...Heat-related illnesses increase significantly during
periods of very high heat indices or high temperatures. This
extreme heat event poses a severe threat to anyone with inadequate
cooling or hydration. These extreme impacts will be most pronounced
across coastal sections, lowlands, interior valleys, and urban
areas.
properties.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

Do not leave young children and pets in unattended vehicles. Car
interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

properties.description:

with moderate levels of humidity will produce heat indices near 105
this afternoon across much of the South Carolina Lowcountry and
Southeast Georgia. Those participating in outside September 11th
memorial activities should be prepared for this level of heat and
humidity today.

Scattered showers and thunderstorms will produce relief in some areas
later today. Cloud-to-ground lightning will pose a risk to anyone
caught outdoors. Be prepared to seek shelter should thunderstorms
approach. Remember, When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors!
properties.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sunshine, and check up on relatives and neighbors.

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and
heat stroke.

Lightning can strike 15 miles away from a thunderstorm. Seek safe
shelter inside a building or vehicle should thunderstorms approach.

* IMPACTS...Heat related illnesses increase significantly during
extreme heat events. Overexposure can cause heat cramps and heat
exhaustion to develop and, without intervention, can lead to heat

properties.instruction:
An Extreme Heat Warning means that a period of very hot temperatures,
even by local standards, will occur. Actions should be taken to
lessen the impact of the extreme heat.

Take extra precautions if you work or spend time outside. When
possible, reschedule strenuous activities to early morning or
evening. Know the signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion and heat
stroke. Wear lightweight and loose-fitting clothing when possible and
drink plenty of water.

To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety and
Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

Public cooling shelters are available in some areas. Consult county
officials for more details.

properties.headline: Hydrologic Outlook issued September 10 at 3:42PM AKDT by NWS Anchorage AK
properties.description:
ESFAFC

UPDATE: Based on forecast winds and water levels, flooding continues
to look very unlikely along Kuskokwim River and the coast. However,
higher water levels and winds gusting up to 30 to 45 mph may still
impact activities along the water.

For communities along Kuskokwim River (Tuntutuliak):
* Gusty winds and storm surge pushing up the river will likely cause
water levels to reach bankfull.
* Flooding will be very unlikely as high water currently in McGrath
and Crooked Creek is now forecast to arrive in the lower Kuskokwim
River after the storm surge has subsided.
* Timing: Water levels will be highest during high tide, which will
be from around 11 AM through 3 PM on Friday.

For communities along the coast (Kongiganak, Kwigillingok, Kipnuk,
Toksook Bay, Tununak):
* Though there will be gusty onshore winds and storm surge, water
levels will very likely remain below 1 to 2 feet above the normal
highest tide, with no flooding expected.
* Timing: Water levels will be highest during high tide on Friday,
from about 10 AM through 2 PM. Communities further north (like
Toksook Bay and Tununak) may see higher water levels during
Thursday nights high tide as well, from about 10 PM through 2 AM.

Next steps:
* Use caution along Kuskokwim River and along the coast, and plan for
higher than normal water levels.
* Send weather or flooding reports to inws.ncep.noaa.gov/report/ or
by calling 1-907-266-5127.
